overview.text: The phrase “U.S. national parks” is often used broadly for places in the National Park System, managed by the National Park Service (NPS), a federal bureau in the Department of the Interior. These places protect scenic and scientifically important natural features—such as forests, deserts, rivers, geological formations and wildlife—as well as sites important to history and culture. Their official names vary: the system includes national parks, monuments, preserves, historic sites, seashores and other designations, so not every unit is titled a national park. Congress established Yellowstone in 1872 as the first federally protected national park, setting it aside for public benefit and enjoyment; the NPS was created later, in 1916.

key_facts.text: The National Park Service was created on August 25, 1916, to manage national parks and monuments then under the Department of the Interior.
National Park System units have many official designations, including national parks, monuments, preserves, historic sites, seashores and battlefields.
Natural areas in the system may protect forests, deserts, rivers, geological features and wildlife, and may be valued for scenic or scientific qualities.
The system also protects places that preserve or commemorate people, events and activities important in U.S. history.
Congress established Yellowstone on March 1, 1872, dedicating it as a public park for the benefit and enjoyment of the people.
